source: South-eastward from the Cape, off the distant Crozetts, a good cruising ground for Right Whalemen, a sail loomed ahead, the Goney (Albatross) by name. As she slowly drew nigh, from my lofty perch at the fore-mast-head, I had a good view of that sight so remarkable to a tyro in the far ocean fisheries—a whaler at sea, and long absent from home.

As if the waves had been fullers, this craft was bleached like the skeleton of a stranded walrus. All down her sides, this spectral appearance was traced with long channels of reddened rust, while all her spars and her rigging were like the thick branches of trees furred over with hoar-frost. Only her lower sails were set. A wild sight it was to see her long-bearded look-outs at those three mast-heads. They seemed clad in the skins of beasts, so torn and bepatched the raiment that had survived nearly four years of cruising. Standing in iron hoops nailed to the mast, they swayed and swung over a fathomless sea; and though, when the ship slowly glided close under our stern, we six men in the air came so nigh to each other that we might almost have leaped from the mast-heads of one ship to those of the other; yet, those forlorn-looking fishermen, mildly eyeing us as they passed, said not one word to our own look-outs, while the quarter-deck hail was being heard from below.
“Ship ahoy! Have ye seen the White Whale?”

But as the strange captain, leaning over the pallid bulwarks, was in the act of putting his trumpet to his mouth, it somehow fell from his hand into the sea; and the wind now rising amain, he in vain strove to make himself heard without it. Meantime his ship was still increasing the distance between. While in various silent ways the seamen of the Pequod were evincing their observance of this ominous incident at the first mere mention of the White Whale’s name to another ship, Ahab for a moment paused; it almost seemed as though he would have lowered a boat to board the stranger, had not the threatening wind forbade. But taking advantage of his windward position, he again seized his trumpet, and knowing by her aspect that the stranger vessel was a Nantucketer and shortly bound home, he loudly hailed—“Ahoy there! This is the Pequod, bound round the world! Tell them to address all future letters to the Pacific ocean! and this time three years, if I am not at home, tell them to address them to ——”

At that moment the two wakes were fairly crossed, and instantly, then, in accordance with their singular ways, shoals of small harmless fish, that for some days before had been placidly swimming by our side, darted away with what seemed shuddering fins, and ranged themselves fore and aft with the stranger’s flanks. Though in the course of his continual voyagings Ahab must often before have noticed a similar sight, yet, to any monomaniac man, the veriest trifles capriciously carry meanings.

“Swim away from me, do ye?” murmured Ahab, gazing over into the water. There seemed but little in the words, but the tone conveyed more of deep helpless sadness than the insane old man had ever before evinced. But turning to the steersman, who thus far had been holding the ship in the wind to diminish her headway, he cried out in his old lion voice,—“Up helm! Keep her off round the world!”

Round the world! There is much in that sound to inspire proud feelings; but whereto does all that circumnavigation conduct? Only through numberless perils to the very point whence we started, where those that we left behind secure, were all the time before us.

Were this world an endless plain, and by sailing eastward we could for ever reach new distances, and discover sights more sweet and strange than any Cyclades or Islands of King Solomon, then there were promise in the voyage. But in pursuit of those far mysteries we dream of, or in tormented chase of that demon phantom that, some time or other, swims before all human hearts; while chasing such over this round globe, they either lead us on in barren mazes or midway leave us whelmed.

modern_en.title: Chapter 52 — The Albatross
paragraphs: Southeastward from the Cape, off the distant Crozets — a good cruising ground for Right Whalemen — a sail appeared ahead: the Goney, or Albatross by name. As she slowly drew near, from my lofty perch at the foremast-head I had a good view of that sight so remarkable to a newcomer in the far ocean fisheries: a whaler at sea, long absent from home.

This vessel was bleached like the skeleton of a stranded walrus, as though the waves had been fullers whitening cloth. All down her sides this ghostly look was streaked with long runs of reddened rust, and all her spars and rigging looked like the thick branches of trees furred with hoarfrost. She carried only her lower sails. Her long-bearded lookouts at the three mastheads were a wild sight. They seemed to be dressed in animal skins, so ragged and patched were the clothes that had lasted through nearly four years of cruising. They stood in iron hoops nailed to the mast, swaying and swinging over a bottomless sea; and when the ship glided slowly in close under our stern, we six men aloft came so near one another that we could almost have jumped from one ship's mastheads to the other's. Yet those forlorn-looking fishermen, watching us mildly as they went by, never said a word to our lookouts, while below, the hail from the quarter-deck rang out.
"Ship ahoy! Have you seen the White Whale?"

But as the strange captain, leaning over the pale bulwarks, was in the act of putting his trumpet to his mouth, it somehow fell from his hand into the sea; and with the wind now rising hard, he tried in vain to make himself heard without it. Meanwhile his ship was still widening the distance between us. While the seamen of the Pequod were showing in various silent ways that they had marked this ominous incident at the very first mention of the White Whale's name to another ship, Ahab paused for a moment; it almost seemed as though he would have lowered a boat to board the stranger, had not the threatening wind forbidden it. But taking advantage of his windward position, he seized his trumpet again, and, knowing by her look that the stranger was a Nantucketer and shortly bound home, he hailed loudly — "Ahoy there! This is the Pequod, bound round the world! Tell them to address all future letters to the Pacific Ocean! And this time three years, if I am not at home, tell them to address them to ——"

At that moment the two ships' wakes were fairly crossed, and instantly — as was their strange custom — schools of small harmless fish that had been peacefully swimming alongside us for some days darted away with what seemed shuddering fins, and ranged themselves fore and aft along the stranger's flanks. Though in the course of his continual voyaging Ahab must often have noticed a similar sight before, to any monomaniac man the merest trifles capriciously carry meanings.

"Swim away from me, do you?" murmured Ahab, gazing over into the water. There seemed little in the words, but the tone conveyed more deep helpless sadness than the mad old man had ever before shown. But turning to the helmsman, who had been holding the ship into the wind to slow her progress, he cried out in his old lion's voice — "Up helm! Keep her off round the world!"

Round the world! There is much in that sound to inspire proud feelings. But where does all that circumnavigation lead? Only through numberless dangers to the very point where we started, where those we left behind — safe and secure — were all the time ahead of us.

If this world were an endless plain, and by sailing east we could keep reaching new distances forever, and discover sights sweeter and stranger than any Cyclades or Islands of King Solomon, then the voyage would hold promise. But when we pursue those distant mysteries we dream of, or chase in torment that demon phantom which sooner or later swims before every human heart — when we chase such things around this round globe, they either lead us on through barren mazes or leave us swamped halfway.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 52 — Albatrossen
paragraphs: Sydøst for Kap det Gode Håb, ud for de fjerne Crozet-øer — en god krydsningsplads for rethvalfangere — dukkede et sejl op forude: Goney eller Albatros ved navn. Mens hun langsomt kom nærmere, havde jeg fra min høje udkigspost i formastet et godt udsyn til det syn, der er så bemærkelsesværdigt for en nykommer i de fjerne havfiskerier: en hvalfanger på havet, som længe har været borte hjemmefra.

Dette skib var bleget som skelettet af en strandet hvalros, som om bølgerne havde været valkere, der blegede klæde. Ned ad hele hendes sider var dette spøgelsesagtige udseende stribet af lange render af rødlig rust, og alle hendes rundholter og hele hendes rigning lignede træers tykke grene beklædt med rimfrost. Hun førte kun sine nederste sejl. Hendes langskæggede udkigsmænd på de tre mastetoppe var et vildt syn. De så ud, som om de var klædt i dyreskind, så laset og lappet var det tøj, der havde holdt i næsten fire års krydsen. De stod i jernringe, der var slået fast på masten, og svajede og svingede over et bundløst hav; og da skibet langsomt gled ind tæt under vores hæk, kom vi seks mand i vejret så tæt på hinanden, at vi næsten kunne have sprunget fra det ene skibs mastetoppe over til det andets. Alligevel sagde de fiskere med det forladte udseende ikke et ord til vores udkigsmænd, men så mildt på os, mens de gled forbi, og nede på agterdækket lød råbet.
»Skib ohøj! Har I set den hvide hval?«

Men netop som den fremmede kaptajn, der lænede sig ud over det blege skansekled, var ved at sætte sit råbehorn for munden, faldt det på en eller anden måde ud af hans hånd og i havet; og da vinden nu tog hårdt til, forsøgte han forgæves at gøre sig hørt uden det. Imens øgede hans skib stadig afstanden mellem os. Mens Pequods søfolk på forskellige tavse måder viste, at de havde lagt mærke til denne ildevarslende hændelse, allerede da den hvide hvals navn første gang blev nævnt for et andet skib, standsede Ahab et øjeblik; det var næsten, som om han ville have sænket en båd for at komme om bord på den fremmede, hvis ikke den truende vind havde forbudt det. Men han udnyttede sin position til luvart, greb atter sit råbehorn, og da han på hendes udseende kunne se, at den fremmede var fra Nantucket og snart på vej hjem, råbte han højt: »Ohøj, der! Det her er Pequod, på vej rundt om jorden! Sig, at alle breve fremover skal sendes til Stillehavet! Og om tre år, på denne tid, hvis jeg ikke er hjemme, så sig, at de skal sendes til ——«

I det øjeblik krydsedes de to skibes kølvand, og straks — som deres underlige skik var — fór de stimer af små, uskadelige fisk, som i nogle dage havde svømmet fredeligt ved siden af os, væk med det, der syntes at være dirrende finner, og stillede sig op for og agter langs den fremmedes sider. Selv om Ahab under sine uafbrudte rejser sikkert ofte måtte have set noget lignende før, får selv den mindste bagatel for ethvert monomant menneske lunefuldt en betydning.

»Svømmer I væk fra mig, gør I?« mumlede Ahab og stirrede ud over rælingen ned i vandet. Der syntes ikke meget i ordene, men tonen rummede en dybere, hjælpeløs sorg, end den gale gamle mand nogen sinde før havde vist. Men så vendte han sig til rorgængeren, som havde holdt skibet op i vinden for at dæmpe farten, og råbte med sin gamle løvestemme: »Op med roret! Hold hende af, rundt om jorden!«

Rundt om jorden! Der er meget i den lyd, der vækker stolte følelser. Men hvor fører al den omsejling hen? Kun gennem utallige farer til selve det punkt, hvor vi begyndte, hvor dem, vi forlod — i sikkerhed og tryghed — hele tiden var os forud.

Hvis denne verden var en endeløs slette, og vi ved at sejle østpå kunne blive ved med at nå nye fjerne steder for evigt og opdage syn, der er sødere og mærkeligere end noget på Kykladerne eller Kong Salomons Øer, så ville rejsen rumme et løfte. Men når vi forfølger de fjerne mysterier, vi drømmer om, eller i kval jager det dæmoniske genfærd, som før eller siden svømmer foran ethvert menneskehjerte — når vi jager den slags rundt på denne runde klode, så fører de os enten gennem golde labyrinter eller lader os forlise halvvejs.
